name: Thirumakaraleeswarar Temple, Tirumagaral
deity: Shiva as Thirumakaraleeswarar (Udumbeeswarar), with the goddess Tribuvananayagi
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Thondai country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); present masonry structure of the Nayak period (16th century)
dynasty: Early Chola tradition; rebuilt under the Vijayanagara Nayaks
summary: Thirumakaraleeswarar is the Shiva of the village of Magaral in the Thondai country, the Tirumagaral of Sambandar's hymn, remembered for a lingam shaped like the tail of a monitor lizard and the legend of a king who learned that the creature he chased was the Lord himself.

sections.history: Magaral lies in the quiet farmland between Kanchipuram and Uthiramerur, in the region the old texts call Thondai Nadu. The village is the Tirumagaral of the Tevaram, where the child-saint Sambandar sang a decad to Shiva, a hymn that tradition remembers as one that removes the burden of past deeds. That praise makes the shrine a Paadal Petra Sthalam, and it is counted seventh among the Tevaram temples of the Thondai country. The founding of the temple is credited by tradition to a Chola king, usually named as Rajendra Chola, though the sources do not agree on which ruler is meant, and some speak of an earlier Pallava-era sanctuary. Inscriptions of the later Chola, Pandya and Vijayanagara periods are reported here. The stone temple seen today was raised in the sixteenth century under the Nayak rulers of the Vijayanagara empire, on the site of the older shrine.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian structure entered beneath a five-tiered gopuram, with the usual progression of flagstaff, hall and sanctum that marks the Nayak-era temples of the region. The heart of the shrine is the lingam of Thirumakaraleeswarar, which is unlike most others: it is small and tapering, said to resemble the tail of a monitor lizard, and devotees point out a mark on it that they read as an old scar. The goddess Tribuvananayagi, who is also named Tribhuvaneswari in some accounts, has her own shrine within the enclosure. Among the carvings, devotees draw attention to a sculpture of Murugan riding an elephant, which local tradition connects to the story of the demon Magaran.
sections.legends: The legend of Magaral belongs to a king who was out hunting and saw a golden monitor lizard, an udumbu, dart away from him. He chased it until it vanished into an anthill, and, reaching in, he seized its tail. When his men dug at the mound to bring the creature out, blood was seen flowing from the earth, and the king fell in a faint. A divine voice then spoke to him, telling him that the golden lizard was none other than Shiva and commanding that a temple be built on the spot. The Lord is therefore remembered here as Udumbeeswarar, the Lord of the monitor lizard, and the slender form of the lingam is said to keep the memory of that day. A second tradition ties the village name to a demon, Magaran, destroyed by Murugan, who came from Thirukazhukundram on the elephant Airavata; accounts of this story vary.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps four main festivals through the year, and its most prominent is the Brahmotsavam in the Tamil month of Masi, in February or March, when the deities are carried in procession through the village. Maha Shivaratri, Navaratri, Masi Magam and Vaikasi Visakam are observed with special worship, and the monthly Pradosham is kept as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Magaral is a place for slow, attentive worship rather than crowds. The road from Kanchipuram runs through paddy and village lanes before the gopuram appears, and inside the temple is hushed and unhurried. Take time at the sanctum to look closely at the lingam and its unusual form, then pay respects to Tribuvananayagi in her shrine. Many devotees come with prayers for the ending of troubles, for relief from the burden of old karma as the saint's hymn promises, and for the reunion of couples who have been parted. The village is small, so carry water and plan to make the visit with Kanchipuram's other temples.

visit.timings: Reported to open in the morning, about 7:30 to midday, and again from late afternoon to about 8 pm, with the first daily ritual at around 6 am according to some sources; hours differ between sources, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Magaral lies on the Kanchipuram–Uthiramerur road, about 16 km from Kanchipuram and 12 km from Uthiramerur, reached by way of Orikkai. Kanchipuram is the nearest town with railway connections, and Chengalpattu is the nearest junction. Chennai has the nearest major airport. Buses ply the Kanchipuram–Uthiramerur route; confirm the last stretch locally, and consider a car or auto from Kanchipuram.
